name: Insurance
blurb: Underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection under active regulator supervision, with NAIC, AM Best, and the Evident insurance index.

points.desc: The NAIC model bulletin on insurers' use of AI - adopted by a growing majority of states - is the operative US governance document for the sector.
points.name: NAIC set the supervisory frame

points.desc: Outside-in benchmarking of the major global insurers on AI talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency - the sector's comparative maturity scoreboard.
points.name: The Evident AI Index benchmarks insurers

reading.body:
The operative constraint on insurance AI is regulatory: the NAIC model bulletin, adopted by a growing majority of states, sets algorithmic-fairness expectations for underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection.

The pattern is supervision plus external benchmarking. NAIC appears twice, as the source of the model bulletin and as the body setting model-governance expectations, which makes it the binding layer over underwriting AI. AM Best folds innovation and digital maturity into credit opinion, and the Evident AI Index scores insurers on talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency. Together these measure governance and capability, not model output.

The data does not cover compute, data center capacity, or grid constraints, so it cannot support claims about infrastructure limits on insurance AI. It also gives no adoption counts or performance figures beyond the statement that a growing majority of states have adopted the bulletin. What it establishes is that the sector's AI deployments are named and supervised, with fairness expectations attached to the three core use cases.

summary: Underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection are the deployments regulators are actively supervising.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's survey for finance and insurance (NAICS 52) puts current AI use at 41.0% of firms answering yes to using AI in the last two weeks, up from 36.5% in the prior period. The question was first asked in September 2023. This is the combined finance and insurance sector, so it is a broad proxy rather than an insurance-only measure.

Per NAIC, AI in insurance is deployed across underwriting, pricing, customer service, claims handling, marketing, and fraud detection. Insurers use AI-powered chatbots to answer common customer questions, provide basic information, and assist with simple transactions at any time of day. In claims processing, AI can help estimate repair costs or assess damage using photos and historical data. NAIC also notes that AI tools can analyze large amounts of insurer data quickly to identify patterns, manage risk, and support decision-making, and may help shift the industry from a detect and repair approach to a predict and prevent approach.

NAIC names large language models such as CoPilot, ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini as tools that can answer questions, summarize documents, and assist with writing tasks. It cautions that these tools do not truly understand context and meaning the way humans do and may generate information that sounds accurate but is incorrect, so AI-generated information should be reviewed carefully, especially for important decisions.

Evident benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across financial services and publishes an Evident AI Index for Insurance. Its 2026 results and report explore how leading insurers are adopting, scaling, and embedding AI, and where the technology is starting to unlock value and where insurers should focus next. AM Best evaluates innovation and digital maturity as part of its assessments, with technology capability reaching credit opinion. Neither source in this material reports a quantified return on investment.

On governance, NAIC states that insurers using AI remain responsible for complying with insurance laws, regulations, insurance standards, and consumer protection rules, including requirements related to fairness, accuracy, and avoiding unfair discrimination. State insurance regulators oversee insurers' use of AI and may require companies to explain how these tools are used in underwriting, pricing, marketing, or claims decisions. NAIC formed the Innovation Cybersecurity and Technology (H) Committee in 2021 and the Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (H) Working Group in 2019, which developed regulatory principles adopted at the 2020 Summer National Meeting. Beginning in 2021, NAIC surveyed insurers by line of business, with aggregate reports on private passenger auto, homeowners, life, and health insurance issued in December 2022, August 2023, December 2023, and May 2025.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material suggests AI is more likely to support human workers than replace them entirely. Actuaries, underwriters, claims professionals, agents, and customer service representatives still play an important role in reviewing information, exercising judgment, and working directly with consumers. Human oversight remains an important part of insurance decision-making, and any deployment should anticipate regulatory scrutiny and the need to review AI-generated output carefully.

https://content.naic.org/.brief: The homepage invites users to explore recent publications, the latest news articles, new federal and legislative news, and model laws. It presents these resources as a way to help inform their approach. The page is organized to provide quick access to up-to-date regulatory information. Users can browse the listed materials to stay current with relevant laws and guidance.

https://evidentinsights.com/.brief: Evident Insights is an intelligence platform that benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across the financial services sector. It supplies data, research, and benchmarking to help financial services leaders make informed AI-related decisions, investments, and strategic choices. The platform publishes the Evident AI Index, which ranks banks and insurers on their AI deployment and highlights emerging trends. Since launching in January 2023, the index has sparked debate and received widespread press coverage, with Evident CEO Alexandra Mousavizadeh frequently commenting on global AI trends.

https://content.naic.org/insurance-topic.brief: NAIC created the Innovation Cybersecurity and Technology Committee in 2021 to discuss how new technology, including AI, affects insurance regulation. The Big Data and Artificial Intelligence Working Group, established in 2019, produced regulatory principles on AI that NAIC members adopted in 2020, and has been surveying insurers across lines of business, issuing reports in December 2022, August 2023, December 2023, and May 2025. AI is applied in underwriting, pricing, customer service, claims handling, marketing, and fraud detection, and can help insurers shift from a “detect and repair” approach to a “predict and prevent” strategy. The Working Group notes that while AI can automate many tasks, human oversight remains essential for compliance with fairness, accuracy, and consumer protection rules.
